title: Concept
text:
Concept
Discriminative vs. Generative
• Discriminative: learn p(y | x) or a decision boundary
• Image classification networks (CNN/ViT): pθ(y | x); where y is the class
label (e.g. dog–cat, ImageNet), and x is the input image.
• Generative: learn a distribution over data, usually p(x) or p(x, y) (e.g.
VAE/GAN/DDPM for images learn p(x); class-conditional models such
as cGAN learn something close to p(x, y) or p(x | y)).
Quick reminder about “generation” (sampling from a known distribution)
If the probability distribution is already known, “generation” simply means random sampling from
that distribution, similar to a basic operation in NumPy/PyTorch:
import numpy as np
x_n = np.random.normal(loc=0.0, scale=1.0, size=(4,)) # N(0,1)
x_u = np.random.uniform(low=-1.0, high=1.0, size=(4,)) # U[-1,1]

• Typical datasets: MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, CelebA, ImageNet

title: Families of image generators
text:
Families of image generators
High-level landscape
• Autoencoders (AE): encoder x 7→z, decoder z 7→ˆx (typically a
deterministic bottleneck).
• Variational Autoencoders (VAE): probabilistic AE with latent prior
p(z) and ELBO training.
• Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN): generator G(z) vs.
discriminator D(x) in a minimax game.
• Diffusion / score-based models: gradually add noise then learn to
reverse the process.
• Autoregressive models: factorize p(x) pixel-by-pixel (PixelCNN,
PixelRNN).

title: Data protocol
text:
Data protocol
Train / validation / test (MNIST)
• Official MNIST training set (60,000 images) is split into:
• train fraction = train ratio (e.g. 0.8–0.9) for optimization,
• validation = remainder, for model selection (best checkpoint).
• Official MNIST test set (10,000) is held out for final evaluation only
(same spirit as the RNN MNIST demo).
• All three demos normalize pixels consistently where needed (e.g. VAE:
[0, 1]; GAN / diffusion: often [−1, 1] for Tanh or Gaussian noise).

title: VAE
text:
VAE
Two terms in words (before heavy math)
• Reconstruction: make ˆx close to x (in code: often BCE with sigmoid
pixels, or MSE under a Gaussian decoder).
• Regularization: keep qϕ(z | x) close to prior p(z) so latents stay in a
region where sampling works — implemented as KL divergence.
• Trade-off: fidelity vs. structured latent space (often weighted by β in
β-VAE).
• Reparameterization: sample z so gradients reach encoder parameters
(derived in the mathematical view).

title: Why VAE samples often look “soft”
text:
Why VAE samples often look “soft”
Beyond “train longer”
• Factorized likelihood / ELBO can favor averages across plausible shapes
⇒blurry edges.
• More epochs help only partly; perceptual sharpness is not the main
selling point vs. GANs / diffusion.

title: DDPM

Why diffusion is attractive
• Stable training objective: supervised noise prediction (MSE-style), no
adversarial minimax game.
• High sample quality: often competitive visual fidelity.
• Trade-off: generation is slower because sampling needs many reverse

• GAN = fast generation, harder training.
• Diffusion = easier training, slower generation.

title: DDPM for beginners
text:
DDPM for beginners
Minimum you must remember
1 Forward noising: gradually add Gaussian noise to clean image x0 until
almost pure noise xT.
2 Train target: given (xt, t), the model predicts the injected noise ϵ.
3 Loss: simple regression loss (typically MSE/L2) between true noise and
predicted noise.
4 Generation: start from xT ∼N(0, I), denoise step-by-step to get x0.
5 Trade-off: usually stable and high quality, but sampling is slower than
one-shot generators.
One-line memory
DDPM = “add noise with a known rule” + “learn to remove it step-by-step.”
